title: Mitochondrial Respiratory Chain Function in Multiple System Atrophy
ops: Mitochondrial Respiratory Chain Function in Multiple System Atrophy

\*M. Gu, \*M. T. Gash, \*J. M. Cooper, †G. K. Wenning, ‡S. E. Daniel, †N. P. Quinn, †C. D. Marsden, and \*†A. H. V. Schapira
\*Department of Clinical Neurosciences, Royal Free Hospital School of Medicine, †University Department of Clinical Neurology, Institute of Neurology, and ‡Parkinson's Disease Society Brain Bank, London, England

Multiple system atrophy (MSA) is a clinicopathological entity distinct from idiopathic Parkinson's disease (PD) that is responsible for 5–10% of cases of parkinsonism. Degeneration of nigral neurones is a feature of both diseases. A specific deficiency of mitochondrial complex I activity has been found in PD substantia nigra. We have analysed mitochondrial function in substantia nigra and platelets from MSA patients to identify any respiratory chain defect in this disorder and to determine its tissue specificity. As our MSA patients had been on L-DOPA, we also sought to establish whether this treatment could cause the complex I defect as seen in PD. We found no

significant difference in respiratory chain activity corrected for mitochondrial mass between control and MSA patients in either of the tissues studied. These results provide a biochemical dimension to the differences between MSA and idiopathic PD. In addition, the fact that L-DOPA failed to induce a complex I defect in MSA substantia nigra suggests that this treatment is unlikely to cause the complex I deficiency in PD, without additional factors that may operate in PD. Key Words: Multiple system atrophy—Mitochondria—L-DOPA.

Multiple system atrophy (MSA) is a distinct sporadic adult-onset neurodegenerative disorder characterized clinically by autonomic failure, parkinsonism, cerebellar ataxia, and pyramidal signs in any combination and pathologically by cell loss and gliosis in a selection of the following structures: substantia nigra, locus ceruleus, striatum, olives, pons, cerebellum, intermediolateral cell columns, and Onuf's nucleus of the spinal cord. A characteristic cytological marker for MSA (the glial cytoplasmic inclusion) was described in 1989 (1). MSA accounts for $\sim$ 10% of patients with parkinsonism in specialized brain banks and represents the most common cause of parkinsonism after Parkinson's disease (PD) (2).
The cause of neuronal death in MSA is unknown.

MSA and PD share some important clinical and pathological features (Table 1), in particular, progressive nigral dopaminergic cell loss, suggesting the possibility of similar mechanisms of cell death. The neurotoxin 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP) has been shown to destroy substantia nigral neurones probably through its ability to inhibit mitochondrial complex I activity and generate free radicals. The discovery of complex I deficiency in the substantia nigra in PD (3,4) suggested a direct biochemical link between the idiopathic disease and the MPTP model. The relevance of this biochemical defect to the cause of dopaminergic cell death in PD is enhanced by the finding that the complex I deficiency is confined to the substantia nigra within the brain and is not present in the caudate nucleus, putamen, globus pallidus, cerebral cortex, or cerebellum (see ref. 5 for review). Activities of the other respiratory chain complexes (II/III and IV) were not significantly different from those of age-matched controls in any of the brain areas examined, including the substantia nigra. To understand the biological underpinnings of these clinical differences, researchers have looked beyond the surface symptoms to the cellular machinery. Specifically, mitochondrial
been considered as a potential cause for the neuronal loss in MSA.
Think of mitochondria as the power plants of the cell; if they fail, the cell dies.

To investigate the potential contribution of mitochondrial dysfunction to the pathogenesis of MSA and determine its tissue specificity, we investigated substantia nigra and platelet mitochondrial respiratory chain function in MSA patients and matched controls.

Why look at platelets? Platelets are small, non-nucleated fragments of blood cells that are abundant and easy to obtain from a simple blood draw. Because they share a common embryonic origin with certain neural tissues and contain mitochondria, they serve as a convenient "window" into the metabolic state of the nervous system without requiring invasive brain surgery.
In addition, most MSA patients are given L-DOPA, and so this disease can provide information on whether this drug can induce the complex I defect observed in PD.

This is a critical question: does the drug treat the disease, or does it potentially contribute to the damage? By studying MSA, where L-DOPA is less effective and the pathology is distinct, we can isolate the effects of the drug from the disease process itself.
The first step in our investigation was to secure high-quality biological samples.
half were formalin fixed for neuropathological examination, while the remaining half were frozen, initially at $-20^{\circ}$ C and subsequently at $-70^{\circ}$ C, for biochemical assay.

This dual approach is essential: formalin fixation preserves the structural architecture of the tissue, allowing pathologists to see *where* cells are lost, while deep freezing preserves the delicate chemical integrity of proteins and enzymes, allowing biochemists to measure *how well* the cellular machinery is functioning.

Mitochondrial respiratory chain function was assayed in homogenates of substantia nigra from 8 control subjects and 8 MSA patients, matched for refrigeration and postmortem delay, and added to our cumulative data on 33 controls and 7 MSA patients to produce substantia nigra data on a total of 41 controls and 15 MSA patients. The cumulative control data were collected using identical assay conditions and techniques.

Matching for "postmortem delay" is a crucial control variable; the longer a brain sits after death, the more enzymes degrade. By ensuring the time between death and freezing was similar for both groups, we ensure that any differences we see are due to the disease, not the timing of the autopsy.

A pathological diagnosis of MSA was based on an appropriate clinical history (2) with the finding of cell loss and gliosis in the absence of Lewy bodies in substantia nigra and striatum with widespread oligodendroglial cytoplasmic inclusions on Bielschowsky silver impregnation or anti-ubiquitin staining.

Let's unpack this diagnostic criteria. "Gliosis" refers to the scarring of the brain tissue (astrocytes) that occurs after neurons die. The "absence of Lewy bodies" is a key differentiator from Parkinson's Disease (PD), which is defined by the presence of these protein aggregates. Instead, MSA is characterized by "oligodendroglial cytoplasmic inclusions" (GCIs). Oligodendrocytes are the cells that wrap around nerve fibers to provide insulation (myelin). Finding inclusions in these cells, visualized using specific stains like Bielschowsky silver or anti-ubiquitin (a protein that tags damaged proteins for disposal), confirms the specific pathology of MSA.

Brain homogenates were prepared and mitochondrial respiratory chain activity and protein content determined as described elsewhere (6). NADH CoQ $_{1}$ reductase (complex I), succinate cytochrome c reductase (complexes II and III), cytochrome oxidase (complex IV), and citrate synthase activities were assayed in triplicate by standard techniques (6,7).

Here we are measuring the "respiratory chain," the series of protein complexes embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane that generate energy.
*   **Complex I (NADH CoQ$_{1}$ reductase):** The first major entry point for electrons.
*   **Complexes II and III (Succinate cytochrome c reductase):** A combined measure of the next two steps in the electron transport chain.
*   **Complex IV (Cytochrome oxidase):** The final step where electrons are passed to oxygen.
*   **Citrate synthase:** This enzyme is part of the Krebs cycle (TCA cycle), which occurs in the mitochondrial matrix. It is used as a "loading control." If citrate synthase levels are low, it means there are fewer mitochondria in the sample, not necessarily that the respiratory chain enzymes are broken.
The values for control (n = 22 and 19) and MSA (n = 7) complex II/III and IV activities in substantia nigra have been published previously (8,9).

Details of pharmacological treatment were available from the MSA patients whose brains were examined postmortem. Fourteen patients were known to have taken L-DOPA during their lifetime for a mean period of 4.2 years (range 1–12 years) with a mean disease duration of 6.9 years. Ten were taking L-DOPA up to the time of death, with a mean daily dose of 550 mg (range 50–1,200 mg).

Tracking this history is vital for the "drug effect" hypothesis mentioned earlier. We need to know who took the drug, for how long, and at what dose to correlate any observed mitochondrial defects with L-DOPA exposure.

Seven patients with MSA were identified according to the clinical criteria of Quinn (2). Four patients were taking L-DOPA (mean dose 400 mg/day, range 250–600 mg). MSA patients were compared with age-and sex-matched control subjects with no evidence of neurological disease. Platelet mitochondria were prepared and assays of respiratory chain enzyme activity were performed as described (10). Statistical analysis was performed using the Mann–Whitney U test.

The Mann–Whitney U test is a non-parametric statistical test used when the data does not follow a normal distribution (a bell curve). Given the small sample sizes and the biological variability of enzyme assays, this is a robust choice for comparing the two groups.

In MSA substantia nigra, there was a significant decrease in the activities of all respiratory chain enzymes, NADH CoQ $_{1}$ reductase (23%), succinate cytochrome c reductase (25%), and cytochrome oxidase (35%) as well as citrate synthase (28%), when enzyme results were expressed per unit total protein (Table 2).

There was severe neuronal loss and degeneration in MSA substantia nigra, which was probably reflected in a decrease in mitochondrial numbers and in the activities of all the mitochondrial enzymes measured. Thus, respiratory chain activities expressed per unit protein will be less in tissues with fewer mitochondria even though the enzymes themselves may be functioning

To understand why this step is necessary, consider that the "raw" numbers in Table 2 represent the total activity of an enzyme per milligram of total protein. However, if a patient’s brain tissue has fewer mitochondria overall, the total enzyme activity will naturally be lower, not necessarily because the individual mitochondria are broken, but simply because there are fewer of them. To distinguish between a *loss* of mitochondria and a *dysfunction* of the remaining mitochondria, scientists use a "normalizer." Citrate synthase is an enzyme located in the mitochondrial matrix that is generally stable and correlates well with total mitochondrial mass. By dividing the activity of the respiratory chain complexes (I, II/III, and IV) by the activity of citrate synthase, we effectively ask: "For every unit of mitochondrial mass present, how efficiently is the respiratory chain working?" When we apply this correction, the apparent deficits seen in the raw data disappear. This indicates that the mitochondria in the substantia nigra of MSA patients are functioning normally on a per-mitochondrion basis, even if the total amount of mitochondrial protein is slightly reduced.

For the substantia nigra samples, the mean age of the MSA group was significantly different from the cumulative control group age (7.2 years; p < 0.02). Thus, we have taken data from controls (n = 22) who match the age range of the MSA group and used these for an additional comparison (Table 4). These data show that with correction for age, there is again no statistically significant difference between the citrate synthase-corrected results for complex I in MSA brain when compared with control brain. This fits with our observation that within the age groups analysed, there is no decline of complex I activity in substantia nigra.

Here, we encounter a critical confounding variable: age. Mitochondrial function naturally declines as we get older. In the initial comparison, the MSA patients were, on average, about 7 years younger than the control group. If we compare a younger disease group to an older healthy group, we might mistakenly attribute age-related changes to the disease, or vice versa. To ensure a fair comparison, we must "match" the groups. By selecting a subset of control subjects whose ages align with the MSA patients, we isolate the effect of the disease from the effect of aging. The result is reassuring: even after accounting for this age difference, the specific activity of Complex I (normalized for mitochondrial mass) remains statistically indistinguishable between MSA patients and healthy controls. This suggests that the core enzymatic machinery of the electron transport chain is not intrinsically defective in the substantia nigra of MSA patients within this age range.

Figure 1 shows the relationship of substantia nigra complex I activity to the mean L-DOPA dose taken by the MSA patients (n = 14) during the last 3 months of life. There is no significant correlation between these two parameters, supporting our general obser-
vation that L-DOPA does not cause a decrease in complex I function in MSA. A similar correlation between L-DOPA dose and substantia nigra complex I activity in PD (n = 38) also failed to show any relationship (data not shown).

A common concern in neurodegenerative research is whether long-term treatment with L-DOPA, a standard therapy for Parkinsonian symptoms, might have toxic side effects on mitochondrial function. To test this, we looked at the patients who were taking L-DOPA and measured their dosage against their Complex I activity. If L-DOPA were damaging the mitochondria, we would expect to see a negative correlation: higher doses would lead to lower enzyme activity. However, the data shows no such relationship. This is a crucial finding because it helps rule out medication-induced mitochondrial toxicity as a primary driver of the pathology in MSA. Furthermore, this finding is consistent with similar observations in Parkinson’s Disease (PD), reinforcing the idea that L-DOPA itself is not the culprit behind mitochondrial dysfunction in these conditions.

Platelet Studies
Mitochondrial respiratory chain function in MSA platelets did not differ significantly from control whether results were expressed per unit protein or corrected for citrate synthase concentration.

Why study platelets? Platelets are cell fragments circulating in the blood that contain mitochondria. Because they are easily accessible via a simple blood draw, they serve as a "peripheral biomarker" or a window into the systemic mitochondrial health of the patient. If MSA were a systemic mitochondrial disorder affecting all tissues, we would expect to see defects in platelets as well. The fact that platelet mitochondrial function is normal in MSA patients suggests that the mitochondrial issues, if they exist, may be localized to specific brain regions like the substantia nigra, or that the systemic mitochondrial machinery remains intact despite the neurological symptoms.

These studies have failed to identify any citrate synthase-corrected mitochondrial abnormality in MSA substantia nigra or platelets.

The table compares two groups: a **Control** group (healthy individuals) and an **MSA** group (patients with Multiple System Atrophy). The sample sizes ($n$) are 22 for controls and 15 for MSA patients. The demographic data shows that the groups are well-matched in terms of age (averaging around 63–65 years) and postmortem delay (the time between death and tissue analysis, averaging around 17–21 hours), which is crucial for ensuring that any differences

The core of the analysis lies

the mitochondrial enzyme activities. **Complex I** is a massive protein complex in the inner mitochondrial membrane responsible for the first step of the electron transport chain, a process vital for generating cellular energy (ATP).

simply measuring Complex I activity per milligram of protein can be misleading. Why? Because in neurodegenerative diseases, neurons die, and the remaining tissue often undergoes **gliosis** (the proliferation of glial cells, which are support cells in the brain). If neurons are lost, the total amount of protein in the sample might change, or the ratio of neuronal to glial protein might shift. To account for this, scientists use a "normalizer" or "control enzyme."

In this study, that normalizer is **Citrate Synthase (CS)**. CS is an enzyme involved in the Krebs cycle (another key energy-producing pathway) that is generally considered stable and unaffected by the specific mitochondrial defects seen in these diseases. By calculating the ratio of **Complex I/CS**, researchers can determine if the Complex I activity is truly deficient relative to the overall metabolic capacity of the tissue, rather than just appearing low because there is less total protein.

Looking at the results in Table 4, we see that while the raw Complex I activity per mg protein is slightly lower in the MSA group (2.69) compared to controls (3.33), the difference is not statistically significant. More importantly, when we look at the **Complex I/CS ratio** (the more rigorous measure), the values are nearly identical: 3.24 in controls versus 3.00 in MSA patients. This indicates that, biochemically, the mitochondrial respiratory chain in the substantia nigra of MSA patients is functioning normally.
